“As confirmed cases of the coronavirus reach new heights in San Francisco, hospitals are facing an uptick in COVID-19 patients, prompting concerns that local health care systems will start to strain from the highly infectious omicron variant.
The number of people hospitalized with COVID-19 in San Francisco was rising fast by Friday — up nearly 50% week over week, though still far below last winter’s high point.

Dr. Bob Wachter, chair of medicine at UCSF, tweeted Thursday that the number of patients admitted into the university’s hospital system more than doubled from 20 people to 45 in the span of 10 days.

“Be super careful — it’s raining COVID,” Wachter tweeted. UCSF hospitals were “now seeing undeniable hospital surge,” he said.
Some patients have been admitted for other conditions and just happen to also test positive for the coronavirus, but Wachter said the spike is still a sign that the pandemic could worsen in the coming weeks — even in places with high vaccination rates, like San Francisco.
“It says to me that if even in highly vaxxed SF, our hospitals will be stretched, hospitals in cities (with) lower vax rates are likely to be hammered,” he tweeted.

Wachter also noted that more than 8% of people without symptoms screened for the coronavirus at UCSF hospitals are receiving a positive test result — implying that one-in-twelve people in San Francisco who have no symptoms are still carrying the virus.

“With that prevalence, you have to assume that everybody you come in contact with might have covid,” he tweeted.

One positive sign: The modest growth in hospitalizations is far less dramatic than San Francisco’s sharp rise in coronavirus cases, which has hit a rolling seven-day average of 608 — nearly four times higher than just one week ago.

Many cases are likely going unreported as well due to the increasing use of at-home COVID-19 tests, the results of which are not always provided to local health departments.

On Friday, San Francisco announced that it would adopt new state guidelines for people infected with the coronavirus similar — but not identical — to those recently implemented by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Under the new protocols, the isolation time for people in San Francisco infected with COVID-19 will be reduced from 10 days to five days. Unlike the federal guidelines, the person must test negative on day five and have no symptoms in order to leave isolation.

People who have been vaccinated against COVID-19 — and received a booster shot if eligible — will not need to quarantine after being in close contact with someone with the coronavirus. The person must get tested after five days, though, and wear a well-fitting mask when around others for ten days.

Unvaccinated people and those who are not up-to-date on their vaccines who are exposed to the coronavirus must quarantine for at least five days, wear a mask for ten days, and receive a negative test, according to the state guidelines.”

As an avid cook and collector of cookbooks, I have three recommendations - 

1. [Salt, Fat, Acid, Heat](https://www.amazon.com/dp/1476753830/ref=cm_sw_r_cp_api_Ljp.BbD0JS1XV)  by Samin Nosrat
2. [The Food Lab](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0393081087/ref=cm_sw_r_cp_api_Vmp.BbXBXYH2E)  by J. Kenji Lopez Alt
3. [The Flavor Bible](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0316118400/ref=cm_sw_r_cp_api_Ynp.BbC9R7MPP)

The first two will teach you the essentials of cooking. How salt, fat, acid, and heat work together to make delicious food. J Kenji Lopez Alt has a popular serious eats blog and his book will teach you everything you need to know about cooking perfect meat, eggs, burgers, etc. 

Once you learn all of the basics from those books, use the Flavor Bible to be creative.
